questions.text: What does embodied energy mean in the audited green-building source?

options.text: Energy used to harvest, manufacture, prepare, and transport materials to a construction site
Only the electricity used by occupants after move-in
Only the cost of installing finishes
Only the number of workers on site

questions.rationale: Energy used to harvest, manufacture, prepare, and transport materials to a construction site. The audited source supports material life-cycle and embodied-energy principles without unsupported carbon factors or certification point claims.
questions.explanation: While 8-9% is the baseline allocation, a 25% reduction does not automatically equal 25% of all project points. Embodied carbon is one component within the materials credit. BERDE does evaluate embodied carbon and waste management as integrated factors within the materials and emissions categories, not as isolated credits. A 25% embodied carbon reduction is significant but does not guarantee BERDE 5-star certification, which requires overall scoring across all categories (energy, water, waste, indoor environment, innovation). BERDE version 5 allocates 8-9% of total points to sustainable materials credits. A 25% embodied carbon reduction may qualify for additional bonuses within this credit category, though automatic certification is not guaranteed. BERDE allocates 8-9% of points to sustainable materials. Embodied carbon reduction is recognized, but candidates must understand that it is one credit component within the broader green building evaluation framework.

questions.text: Which concrete-related material strategy is supported by the audited source?

options.text: Using recycled aggregate, fly ash, or slag where suitable
Claiming all concrete has zero impact
Replacing design review with a marketing label
Ignoring aggregate contamination

questions.rationale: Using recycled aggregate, fly ash, or slag where suitable. The audited source supports material life-cycle and embodied-energy principles without unsupported carbon factors or certification point claims.
questions.explanation: ASTM C618 covers fly ash, not GGBS. Fly ash replacement rates (15-25%) are lower than GGBS because fly ash lacks cementitious properties. ASTM C33 specifies fine and coarse aggregate gradation, not cement replacement materials. ASTM C150 defines Portland cement composition; GGBS is not a Portland cement product but a supplementary cementitious material meeting its own ASTM C989 standard. GGBS is cooled byproduct slag from iron smelting meeting ASTM C989 specifications. It provides both pozzolanic (silica-based) and cementitious (calcium-based) reactions, allowing higher replacement rates of 30-50% compared to fly ash (15-25%). GGBS (ASTM C989) allows higher cement replacement (30-50%) than fly ash (ASTM C618: 15-25%) because it combines pozzolanic and self-cementing properties. Candidates must match material type to the correct ASTM standard and dosage limits.
questions.code_citation: ASTM C989 Standard Specification for Ground Granulated Blast-Furnace Slag; ASTM C618

questions.rationale: Because chemical content, durability, and embodied energy tradeoffs can still matter. The audited source supports material life-cycle and embodied-energy principles without unsupported carbon factors or certification point claims.
questions.explanation: This reverses the coal source and chemical composition. Class F comes from anthracite/bituminous (not lignite), and Class C comes from lignite/subbituminous (not anthracite). ASTM C618 specifies chemical composition requirements and pozzolanic reactivity, not only particle size. While fineness is a specification, the chemical differences between Class F and C are fundamental. Both Class F and Class C are acceptable for structural concrete when dosed within ASTM C618 limits. The difference in dosage reflects their chemical reactivity, not structural suitability. Class F fly ash (from anthracite/bituminous coal) is 50-70% silica and acts only as a pozzolan, replacing 15-25% cement. Class C (from lignite/subbituminous) contains 20-40% CaO, acts both as a pozzolan and self-cements, and is dosed at 20-35%. Both are suitable for structural concrete within their dosage limits. Class F and C fly ash have different chemical compositions, reactivity rates, and optimal dosage ranges. Candidates must match fly ash type to concrete strength requirements and durability goals.

They automatically satisfy every structural code requirement
They have no transport impact at all
They replace professional review

questions.rationale: They can reduce transportation-related embodied energy when suitable for the application. The audited source supports material life-cycle and embodied-energy principles without unsupported carbon factors or certification point claims.
questions.explanation: This incorrectly assumes the 25% replacement equals 25% carbon reduction by ignoring fly ash's embodied carbon contribution. This assumes fly ash has zero embodied carbon, which is incorrect. All materials have some embodied carbon from processing. Fly ash is a waste product from coal burning, but it has measurable embodied carbon from collection, processing, and transport. Its use reduces net carbon compared to 100% Portland cement. Original binder carbon: 350 kg/m³ × 0.82 = 287 kg CO2e/m³. After 25% replacement: 262.5 kg cement (0.82) + 87.5 kg fly ash (0.12) = 221.1 kg CO2e/m³. Reduction: (287-221.1)/287 ≈ 23%. This accounts for fly ash's own embodied carbon (not zero). Embodied carbon reduction from pozzolanic replacement is never equal to the percentage replacement, because the substitute material (fly ash, slag) has non-zero embodied carbon. Always account for both material carbon values when calculating reduction.

questions.rationale: Avoid exact carbon-per-kilogram claims and answer from audited life-cycle principles. The audited source supports material life-cycle and embodied-energy principles without unsupported carbon factors or certification point claims.
questions.explanation: While RCA can meet ASTM C33 gradation, assuming it meets structural concrete requirements without testing is incorrect. Strength and durability must be verified. RCA's higher absorption makes it unsuitable for many fill applications if water ingress is a concern. Its use is primarily limited to controlled fill and base courses. Cost reduction alone does not justify RCA specification. Applications must match durability, strength, and absorption characteristics to intended use. RCA is acceptable for non-structural uses (fill, base course) when meeting ASTM C33 gradation. RCA exhibits higher absorption (3-8% vs 0.5-1% for virgin) and lower strength, limiting use in structural concrete without testing and strength verification. Recycled concrete aggregates are limited to non-structural applications where absorption and strength losses are acceptable. Candidates must recognize RCA limitations and avoid over-specifying reuse in structural concrete without verification testing.

questions.rationale: Minimize material use and maximize reuse or recycling where appropriate. The audited source supports material life-cycle and embodied-energy principles without unsupported carbon factors or certification point claims.
questions.explanation: 24% is far lower than the actual 76% reduction. Confusing recycled and virgin embodied carbon values is a critical error. While aluminum is lighter and lower-cost than steel, ASTM A496 specifies steel wire reinforcement; aluminum does not meet structural reinforcement standards. Recycled aluminum (2.0 kg CO2e/kg) has significantly lower embodied carbon than virgin (8.24 kg CO2e/kg). Material selection must account for this substantial difference. Reduction: (8.24-2.0)/8.24 ≈ 76%. Aluminum is not suitable for structural concrete reinforcement per ASTM standards. Its high cost and corrosion susceptibility in concrete limit use to non-structural cladding, window frames, and interior finish components. Recycled aluminum reduces embodied carbon by 76% compared to virgin but is unsuitable for structural reinforcement. Candidates must understand material-specific embodied carbon and application limitations.

questions.explanation: Laboratory testing of timber is accurate; negative embodied carbon is a valid concept reflecting carbon sequestration, not measurement error. Timber processing requires energy (drying, milling), which adds positive embodied carbon. The net embodied carbon remains negative because sequestration exceeds processing emissions. Timber sustainability depends on harvest method (sustainable forestry vs clear-cutting), replanting, and transport distance. A negative embodied carbon value does not guarantee ecological soundness. Trees sequester atmospheric CO2 during growth through photosynthesis, storing carbon in cellulose and lignin. Timber retains this stored carbon for the duration of its service life. The negative value (carbon credit) offsets the manufacturing and transport emissions. Negative embodied carbon represents carbon sequestration in organic materials. Candidates must understand that timber stores atmospheric CO2, making it a carbon sink if sustainably harvested and managed.
